title: YouTube and the single-rod contraceptive implant: a content analysis
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of YouTube videos about the single-rod contraceptive implant. Videos were coded by two independent researchers for clinical accuracy and the paper reports a quantitative share of items coded as containing misinformation with a stated denominator (n=6, 26% of patient testimonial videos). This meets the CONTENT inclusion criterion (share of items in a sample classified false/inaccurate).

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language YouTube videos, no country restriction; study run at the University of Pittsburgh, USA)
estimates.measure_type: % of patient testimonial YouTube videos about the contraceptive implant that reported misinformation
estimates.denominator: 23 patient testimonial videos that entered the testimonial analysis (from 52 English-language single-rod implant videos retrieved as the top 20 hits by relevance and by view count for three search terms)
estimates.definition: The testimonial contained factually incorrect statements about the implant, e.g. that the device migrates 'deeper in the skin' over time, or that it can cause liver damage or breast lumps
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given; misinformation is illustrated as claims that 'the device migrated “deeper in the skin” over time and that it can cause liver damage or breast lumps'
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 4 (repeated in the Abstract: 'A minority (26%) reported misinformation.')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent researchers viewed every video in the final sample, with a third researcher adjudicating discrepancies; accuracy judged against clinical knowledge of the contraceptive implant. The only reliability statistic given (Cohen's kappa = 0.81) is for the positive/negative experience classification, not for the misinformation coding.
estimates.moderator_quote: Using the search terms ‘contraceptive implant’, ‘Nexplanon’ and ‘Implanon’, the top 20 results on YouTube by relevance and view count were identified. ... Two independent researchers viewed the final sample of videos and a third researcher reviewed the video in the event of a discrepancy.
estimates.notes: The source_quote is the longest contiguous verbatim span available: the PDF prints this sentence across a two-column break, so 'A minority of patient testimonial videos' sits at the end of one line and 'reported misinformation (n=6, 26%).' begins the next, with the adjacent column's text in between. The full sentence reads 'A minority of patient testimonial videos reported misinformation (n=6, 26%).' and the Abstract states 'A minority (26%) reported misinformation.' The Discussion adds 'Misinformation reported in the videos was rare (n=6, 26%) but included mention of the fact that the device migrated “deeper in the skin” over time and that it can cause liver damage or breast lumps.' The denominator is not stated directly; it is recovered from the paper's own percentages for the same subsample (61% = 14/23 and 39% = 9/23 for the positive/negative split; 22% = 5/23; 26% = 6/23), which imply 23 testimonial videos. The Results text elsewhere reports the testimonials as 'n=24, 46%', and the patient/professional counts are inconsistent between the text (40 patient + 12 professional of 52) and Table 2 (38 + 12 of 50). Videos were English-language with no country restriction, so country is coded Global. Modified DISCERN and Global Quality Scale are reported as medians only and therefore yield no share and no row.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) modified DISCERN reliability (median 3 professional vs 2 patient) and Global Quality Scale (4.25 vs 2.5) scores — quality instruments reported only as medians, with no share of videos above a threshold, so per the rules they produce no share and no row; (2) the 61% of testimonials rated 'positive experiences' and the 39% rated negative — sentiment, not veracity; (3) the side-effect content frequencies (61% unpredictable bleeding, 35% amenorrhoea, 30% pain at insertion, etc.) — topic coverage, not falsity; (4) the professional/patient source split (23%/77%) — provenance, not veracity. Uncertainty: the paper's own counts are internally inconsistent (52 vs 50 videos analysed; 24 vs 23 testimonials), so the 26% is certain but its denominator is inferred; confidence set to medium for that reason.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. YouTube API searched on 26 February 2014 for 'contraceptive implant', 'Nexplanon' and 'Implanon', taking the first 20 hits per term by view count and by relevance; 120 videos retrieved, duplicates (52) and non-English videos (15) excluded, 52-53 analysed, of which 23-24 were patient testimonials. Two independent researchers coded each video, third researcher adjudicated discrepancies; inter-rater agreement on the patient-experience classification Cohen's kappa = 0.81. Analyses in STATA V.12; no response rate applicable (content study). IRB approval from University of Pittsburgh.
rob.item6_quote: Misinformation reported in the videos was rare (n=6, 26%) but included mention of the fact that the device migrated ‘deeper in the skin’ over time and that it can cause liver damage or breast lumps.
rob.item10_quote: A minority of patient testimonial videos reported misinformation (n=6, 26%).
